questions.q: Why does the lesson describe 'reproduction + extension' as often the strongest capstone shape?
options: The reproduction half gives a known target to validate your own competence against, making the project self-correcting before you add your own extension
It is the only capstone shape this course allows
It guarantees a publishable result
It requires no understanding of the original paper at all
questions.explain: The lesson explains that reproduction-first catches methodology problems before you build an extension on a shaky foundation, which is what makes the project self-correcting -- it does not guarantee publication.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a realistic capstone project type in this lesson?
options: Proving a new theorem about quantum complexity classes
Building new physical quantum hardware from scratch
Inventing an entirely new quantum algorithm with no prior basis
A comparative benchmark of two or three error-mitigation techniques on a fixed circuit and device
questions.explain: The lesson lists three realistic types: reproduction + extension, comparative benchmark, and applied algorithm implementation/characterization -- all explicitly scoped below the bar of inventing new algorithms or proving new theorems.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about whether the capstone is expected to be publishable or PhD-dissertation-level novel?
options: The lesson takes no position on this question
It explicitly is NOT expected to be either -- it's meant to be small, complete, and honestly reported
It must match the novelty of a PhD dissertation
It must be publishable in a peer-reviewed journal to pass
questions.explain: The lesson sets this expectation explicitly and honestly: the capstone demonstrates the ability to carry a research question through to a defensible conclusion, not publishable or dissertation-level novelty.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a real constraint to check a candidate topic against before committing?
options: Whether a peer-reviewed journal has already rejected it
Hardware/simulator access, time budget, and current skill level
Whether the topic involves more than 100 qubits
Whether the topic has ever appeared in a popular science article
questions.explain: The lesson lists hardware/simulator access, time budget, current skill level, and having a genuinely answerable question as the real constraints to check -- not qubit count or media coverage.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution against picking a topic where the 'answer' is already certain from pure theory?
options: It echoes Lesson 3's hypothesis-quality criteria -- a good hypothesis needs a real, currently-unknown-to-you answer, not a re-derivation of a known result
Because theoretical results are always wrong
Because this course forbids any theoretical content in the capstone
Because pure theory topics cannot be written up in a report
questions.explain: The lesson directly ties this back to Lesson 3's point that re-deriving a known textbook result is a fine learning exercise but isn't research -- a good capstone hypothesis needs an answer that isn't already certain.
